title: THEY TOLD YOU THAT WITHOUT SPEAKING IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT THE BIBLE ACTUALLY SAYS?
paragraphs: THEY TOLD YOU THAT WITHOUT SPEAKING IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT THE BIBLE ACTUALLY SAYS?

One question from the Apostle Paul could overturn years of spiritual insecurity. What really happened at Pentecost, why not every believer has the same gift, and how Jesus never intended His children to measure their salvation by someone else's spiritual experience.
Imagine standing in a crowded church.
The worship is powerful. Hands are lifted. Tears are falling. People are praying with an intensity you can almost feel in your chest.
Then someone begins speaking in tongues.
Another person follows.
Then another.
The atmosphere changes. Someone declares, “The Holy Spirit is moving!”
You believe them. You desperately want to experience everything God has for you.
So you close your eyes tighter.
You lift your hands higher.
You pray harder.
You wait.
And wait.
But nothing comes out of your mouth except the words you already know.
“Jesus, I love You.”
“Lord, please fill me.”
“Holy Spirit, I need You.”
Then comes the sentence that quietly breaks something inside you.
“If you've really received the Holy Spirit, you'll speak in tongues.”
Suddenly, what began as worship becomes a courtroom.
And you are the one on trial.
You start wondering whether your salvation is genuine. Whether your prayers have reached heaven. Whether God has accepted everyone in the room except you.
Maybe you go home that night feeling spiritually defective.
Maybe you start imitating sounds because you're afraid of disappointing the people praying over you.
Or maybe you stop asking God for anything at all because you've convinced yourself that something must be wrong with you.
But what if the problem isn't your faith?
What if the problem is a conclusion people have drawn from Scripture that Scripture itself does not require?

And what if one of the most important questions the Apostle Paul ever asked about spiritual gifts was written precisely to protect the church from turning one gift into everybody's spiritual measuring stick?
Stay with me.
Because we're going to open the Bible, look at the original Greek, walk into the upper room at Pentecost, and listen carefully to what the apostles actually taught.
Not to diminish the gift of tongues.
Not to attack Christians who speak in tongues.
And certainly not to deny the supernatural work of the Holy Spirit.
But to answer a question that has troubled sincere believers for generations:
Must a person speak in tongues to prove that they have received the Holy Spirit?
The answer matters more than you might realize.
Because whenever we make something a requirement that God has not made a requirement, we risk placing burdens on people whom Christ has called to freedom.
And whenever we dismiss something God has genuinely given, we risk closing our hearts to a gift that Scripture tells us not to forbid.
The truth must protect us from both errors.
And the truth begins in Jerusalem.
Before the noise.
Before the fire.
Before the languages.
Before the church became a movement that would shake the world.
There was a promise.
Jesus had been crucified.
The disciples had watched their Teacher suffer the most humiliating death the Roman Empire could inflict.
Their hopes had been shattered.
Their courage had collapsed.
Peter had denied Him.
Thomas had doubted.
Others had hidden behind locked doors.
And yet the risen Christ stood among these frightened people and spoke of a gift they could never manufacture.
In Acts 1:8, Jesus promised:
“But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me.” (KJV)
Notice what Jesus emphasized.
Power.
Witness.
The coming of the Holy Spirit.
The purpose was not to create a spiritual competition.
The purpose was to empower ordinary, formerly frightened disciples to bear witness to the risen Christ.
Then came Pentecost.
Acts 2 describes a sound from heaven like a rushing mighty wind, tongues appearing like fire, and disciples being filled with the Holy Spirit.
Acts 2:4 says:
“And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “other tongues” is ἑτέραις γλώσσαις (heterais glōssais).
Heterais means “other” or “different.”
Glōssais means “tongues” or “languages,” depending on the context.
And the context here is extraordinarily important.
Acts 2:6 tells us that people from different nations heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
Acts 2:8 records the astonished question:
“And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “tongue” in this verse is διαλέκτῳ (dialektō), referring here to a person's own language or dialect.
These were not simply strange sounds that nobody could recognize.
Luke describes a miraculous event in which people from different linguistic backgrounds understood the mighty works of God in their native languages.
The miracle was not merely that the disciples spoke.
It was that the nations heard.
Think about that.
At Babel, human pride was followed by the confusion of languages and the scattering of people.
At Pentecost, God used different languages to proclaim His mighty works across national and cultural boundaries.
Pentecost did not erase linguistic diversity. It demonstrated that the Gospel could cross it.
And when Peter stood to explain what was happening, his message did not culminate in an invitation to demonstrate spiritual superiority.
It culminated in Jesus.
The Jesus they had crucified.
The Jesus God had raised.
The Jesus now exalted at the Father's right hand.
The Jesus who poured out the promised Holy Spirit.
When the crowd was pierced to the heart, they asked what they should do.
Peter answered in Acts 2:38:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Repent.
Be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
Receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Peter did not say that every individual must produce the same manifestation before they could be recognized as belonging to Christ.
But perhaps you're thinking, “Didn't people speak in tongues when they received the Spirit elsewhere in Acts?”
Yes.
And we must take those passages seriously.
In Acts 10, the Holy Spirit fell upon Cornelius and those hearing Peter's message. The Jewish believers were astonished because the gift of the Spirit had been poured out upon Gentiles.
How did they recognize this extraordinary event?
Acts 10:46 says they heard them speaking with tongues and magnifying God.
In Acts 19:6, when Paul laid hands on certain disciples in Ephesus, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke with tongues and prophesied.
These are genuine biblical accounts.
They matter.
They show that speaking in tongues can accompany the reception or manifestation of the Holy Spirit.
But here is the question we cannot avoid:
Does the fact that tongues accompanied some receptions of the Spirit mean that tongues must accompany every reception of the Spirit?
That is a different claim.
And it requires more than pointing to examples.
It requires demonstrating that the New Testament teaches the experience as a universal requirement.
Consider Acts 8.
When the Samaritans received the Holy Spirit through the ministry of Peter and John, Simon saw that something remarkable had happened.
But Luke does not explicitly tell us what he saw.
Some interpreters suggest that speaking in tongues may have occurred.
That is possible.
But the passage does not say so.
We must distinguish between what the text reports and what we infer.
Now consider Acts 4:31.
Believers were filled with the Holy Spirit, and the recorded result was that they spoke the word of God with boldness.
Tongues are not mentioned.
Or consider Acts 9, where Ananias prayed for Saul to regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.
The account does not report Saul speaking in tongues at that moment.
We know from 1 Corinthians 14:18 that Paul later spoke in tongues extensively.
But Acts 9 does not establish tongues as the immediate evidence of his filling.
The Book of Acts shows the Spirit working in remarkable and varied ways.
And Luke's historical descriptions should not automatically be turned into universal commands without considering the rest of Scripture.
Which brings us to the passage that should make every Christian stop and examine their assumptions.
First Corinthians chapter 12.
Paul is writing to a church overflowing with spiritual activity.
There are gifts.
There are manifestations.
There is enthusiasm.
But there is also pride, division, disorder, and a dangerous tendency to rank believers by their spiritual experiences.
Does that sound familiar?
Some believers appear to be treating particular gifts as signs of greater spiritual importance.
And Paul responds by describing the church as one body with many members.
Different functions.
Different gifts.
One Lord.
One Spirit.
One body.
In 1 Corinthians 12:11, Paul says the one Spirit distributes gifts to each person “severally as he will.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase καθὼς βούλεται (kathōs bouletai) means “as He wills.”
The emphasis is on the Spirit's sovereign distribution.
Not on human pressure.
Not on personal status.
Not on everybody displaying the same gift.
Then Paul asks a series of questions in 1 Corinthians 12:29–30:
“Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?” (KJV)
Now listen carefully to the original Greek behind the question about tongues.
μὴ πάντες γλώσσαις λαλοῦσιν;
Mē pantes glōssais lalousin?
Literally:
“Do all speak in tongues?”
The particle μή (mē) introduces a question that, in this grammatical construction, expects a negative answer.
In other words, Paul is not expecting the Corinthians to shout, “Yes! Everyone!”
The expected answer is:
No.
Not everyone is an apostle.
Not everyone is a prophet.
Not everyone is a teacher.
Not everyone works miracles.
And not everyone speaks in tongues.
This is not a dismissal of tongues.
It is Paul's defense of the Spirit's freedom to distribute different gifts throughout Christ's body.
And here is where the theological discussion deserves honesty.
Some Pentecostal traditions distinguish between tongues as the initial physical evidence of Spirit baptism and the continuing congregational gift of tongues discussed in 1 Corinthians 12.
They argue that Paul's question concerns the latter, while Acts provides a pattern for the former.
That distinction is an important part of their interpretation, and it should be represented fairly.
But the distinction is not explicitly stated in 1 Corinthians 12:30.
Nor does Acts directly command every believer to speak in tongues as the necessary proof of having received the Spirit.

For that reason, many Christians—including many who believe that tongues remain a genuine spiritual gift—conclude that Scripture does not establish tongues as a universal requirement for receiving the Holy Spirit.
And that conclusion becomes even more significant when we read what Paul says earlier in the same chapter.
First Corinthians 12:13 declares:
“For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.” (KJV)
All.
That word matters.
All believers belong to the one body through the Spirit.
Yet within that same Spirit-filled body, Paul explains that not everyone possesses the same gifts.
The Spirit unites believers in Christ without making every believer's spiritual experience identical.
And then Romans 8:9 takes us even deeper.
“Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.” (KJV)
Paul makes the Spirit's presence essential to belonging to Christ.
But he does not identify speaking in tongues as the universal test of that presence.
He directs our attention to the Spirit of Christ.
That means the question is not merely whether you have experienced a particular manifestation.
The deeper question is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Have you turned to Him in repentance and faith?
Are you trusting in His death and resurrection rather than your own righteousness?
Is the Spirit drawing you toward Christ, convicting you of sin, and producing a growing desire to obey Him?
Do not misunderstand.
None of these questions is an invitation to earn salvation by spiritual performance.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Christ, not a reward for producing enough religious evidence.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And Ephesians 1:13 says that believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit when they heard the Gospel of salvation and believed in Christ.
The Greek verb for “sealed” is ἐσφραγίσθητε (esphragisthēte), from a verb meaning to seal or mark as belonging to someone.
Paul's emphasis is on God's action in securing and identifying His people.
He does not add, “provided that every believer speaks in tongues.”
Now imagine what that means for the person who has spent years believing they are spiritually incomplete because they have never experienced this gift.
Imagine the weight beginning to lift.
Not because they have discovered an excuse to ignore the Holy Spirit.
But because they have discovered that the Bible's promises are greater than the expectations of a particular church culture.
Yet there is another danger.
And we need to confront it with equal seriousness.
Some Christians have been so wounded by spiritual pressure that they have begun treating every expression of tongues as suspicious.
Others have mocked sincere believers who practice the gift.
Some have dismissed entire congregations as spiritually immature simply because their worship looks different.
That, too, can become pride.
Paul's correction works in both directions.
In 1 Corinthians 14:39, he says:
“Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues.” (KJV)
Forbid not.
Those words belong in our Bibles just as surely as “Do all speak with tongues?”
We must not demand what Scripture does not universally demand.
And we must not forbid what Scripture explicitly tells the church not to forbid.
The answer is neither coercion nor contempt.
It is biblical discernment.
In 1 Corinthians 14, Paul teaches that the exercise of spiritual gifts in gathered worship must serve the building up of the church.
He emphasizes intelligibility, interpretation, order, and love.
He explains that uninterpreted tongues spoken publicly do not communicate understandable instruction to the congregation.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, he gives practical directions for tongues in church gatherings, including interpretation and restraint when no interpreter is present.
This is not the language of spiritual chaos.
It is the language of a shepherd protecting Christ's people.
The Holy Spirit is not honored when believers are pressured into imitation.
He is not honored when sincere questions are silenced.
He is not honored when spiritual experiences become trophies.
And He is not honored when genuine gifts are mocked merely because they make us uncomfortable.
The Spirit glorifies Jesus.
Jesus Himself said in John 16:14:
“He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you.” (KJV)
There it is.
The center of the entire conversation.
Jesus.
Not the reputation of the person praying.
Not the excitement of the room.
Not the ability to produce an impressive manifestation.
Jesus Christ.
And if we want to understand what the Spirit produces in the life of a believer, we must also listen to Galatians 5:22–23.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
These are described as the fruit of the Spirit.
Not because every believer displays them perfectly.
Not because sanctification happens overnight.
But because the Spirit is transforming God's people into the likeness of Christ.
Someone may speak in tongues and still need to repent of bitterness.
Someone may never speak in tongues and yet display extraordinary patience, sacrificial love, and faithfulness to Jesus.
Neither observation allows us to see infallibly into another person's heart.
But it reminds us that spiritual maturity cannot be reduced to one visible gift.
Paul makes that unmistakably clear in 1 Corinthians 13:1:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη (agapē).
Love.
Not sentimental approval of everything.
Not the refusal to speak truth.
But the self-giving love that reflects the character of Christ.
Paul is using powerful rhetorical language to show that even the most extraordinary spiritual expressions are empty without love.
Imagine possessing a gift that astonishes an entire congregation while refusing to forgive someone who wounded you.
Imagine speaking passionately about the Holy Spirit while humiliating a struggling believer who cannot reproduce your experience.
Imagine defending the supernatural while neglecting the very love that Scripture says must govern the use of spiritual gifts.
Something has gone terribly wrong.
Because the gifts were never given to make us look greater than our brothers and sisters.
They were given to serve the body and glorify its Head.
And the Head is Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article has brought back a memory.
A prayer meeting.
A church service.
A moment when someone told you to repeat sounds until something happened.
A night when you cried because everyone else seemed to receive what you couldn't.
Or perhaps you have been on the other side.
Perhaps you genuinely speak in tongues.
Perhaps God has used that gift in your prayer life, and you have treasured it for years.
But somewhere along the way, you began assuming that Christians who did not share your experience were less surrendered, less spiritual, or less filled.
If so, this is not an invitation to abandon your gift.
It is an invitation to surrender your assumptions to Scripture.
Because loving the Holy Spirit means allowing the Holy Spirit to correct us through the Word He inspired.
And if you have been wounded by careless teaching, you do not need to respond by hardening your heart toward everything supernatural.
You can remain open to all that God genuinely gives while refusing to pretend that He has given something He has not.
You can pray for spiritual gifts.
You can ask God for greater boldness.
You can seek deeper intimacy with Christ.
You can study Scripture, pursue holiness, serve the church, and welcome the Spirit's work without manufacturing an experience to satisfy someone else's expectations.
And if God grants you the gift of tongues, receive it humbly and exercise it biblically.
If He grants you another gift, use it faithfully.
If you are still discerning what gifts He has given you, continue growing in the Word, prayer, fellowship, and service.
You do not need to turn uncertainty into a performance.
There is room for reverence.
There is room for learning.
There is room for honest questions.
There is room for the Spirit's work.
But there is no room for making Christ's people feel spiritually worthless because they do not all have the same gift.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of this entire controversy is how easily it can distract us from the greater miracle.
A sinner becoming a child of God.
A proud heart learning repentance.
A bitter person learning forgiveness.
A frightened disciple becoming courageous.
A broken life being restored through the grace of Jesus Christ.
A person who once loved darkness beginning to love the light.
Do not misunderstand me.
The supernatural gifts of the Spirit matter.
But the greatest news of Christianity is not that God can enable a person to speak a language they never learned.
The greatest news is that the crucified and risen Jesus saves sinners, reconciles them to the Father, and gives His Spirit to those who belong to Him.
The Spirit's gifts are wonderful.
The Savior to whom the Spirit points is infinitely greater.
And maybe that is the truth you needed to hear tonight.
You have been searching for proof that God has not rejected you.
You have been replaying the voices of people who questioned your spiritual life.
You have been comparing your prayers, your tears, your worship, and your experiences with everyone around you.
But the Gospel calls you to look somewhere else.
Look to the cross.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the risen Christ.
Look to the One who died for sinners and rose again.
Your hope is not that you can produce a convincing spiritual manifestation.
Your hope is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
This does not mean that everyone who claims to know Jesus truly belongs to Him. Scripture calls us to examine ourselves, repent, believe, and persevere in faith.
But it does mean that the biblical foundation of salvation is not the possession of one particular spiritual gift.
It is Christ Himself.
If you have never truly surrendered to Jesus, do not hide behind church attendance, religious vocabulary, or even supernatural experiences.
Come to Him.
Repent of your sins.
Trust in His finished work.
Believe that He died and rose again.
Ask Him to forgive you, change you, and lead you by His Spirit.
And if you already belong to Christ but have lived under the crushing fear that you are spiritually inferior because you have never spoken in tongues, return to what God has actually said.
Not what someone assumed.
Not what someone demanded.
Not what someone made you feel.
What Scripture says.
The Spirit gives gifts according to His will.
Not everyone has the same gift.
All who truly belong to Christ have His Spirit.
And every gift must be exercised under the lordship of Jesus, in truth and love.
That is not a weak view of the Holy Spirit.
That is a deeply reverent one.
Because we honor Him best when we allow Him to be God rather than attempting to control His work.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
Have you ever felt pressured to speak in tongues to prove that you were saved or filled with the Holy Spirit?
Or has the Lord used this gift in your life in a way that has deepened your prayer and devotion to Christ?
There is room for both testimonies here.
And if you have been carrying spiritual insecurity for years, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
You do not have to expose a painful experience before you are ready.
But you do not have to pretend you have never struggled, either.
Let's make the conversation a place where believers can speak honestly, disagree respectfully, open their Bibles together, and encourage one another toward Jesus.
Because the church does not need another battlefield built around spiritual superiority.
It needs disciples who love the truth enough to be corrected by it.
And love one another enough to handle that truth with grace.
You may never know who reads it in silence.
You may never know whose hands are trembling as they reach the words of 1 Corinthians 12:30.
You may never know whose tears begin to fall when they discover that the Bible does not require every Christian to possess the same gift.
There is also something I want to share with those who believe this kind of ministry matters.

Every article that brings someone back to Scripture, every devotional that encourages a weary believer, and every resource that helps a person understand the Gospel represents an opportunity to serve others in the name of Jesus.
That is why Gospel Warrior continues to develop and share Christian teaching and discipleship resources.
We want people to encounter biblical truth without unnecessary barriers.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
It is a practical way to support the continued creation and sharing of biblical teaching, free resources, and discipleship materials.
Christ has already accomplished what no amount of money could ever accomplish.
But grateful hearts can choose to participate in Gospel ministry through prayer, sharing, service, and financial generosity.
As Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
Simply an opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry committed to pointing people toward Jesus.
These are small expressions of appreciation for those helping the ministry continue.
You are welcome to read, learn, grow, and share the truth of Christ.
Your prayer matters.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
But before you leave, return with me to that church service where this story began.
The room is still full.
The music is still playing.
People are still praying.
Some are speaking in tongues.
Others are worshiping quietly.
And somewhere in the back stands the person who has spent years wondering whether God has forgotten them.
They lift their eyes.
For the first time, they stop trying to manufacture an experience.
They remember the cross.
They remember the empty tomb.
They remember the promise of the Gospel.
And instead of asking, “Why can't I be like everybody else?” they begin asking a better question.
“Lord Jesus, how can I be faithful to You with everything You have given me?”
That question changes everything.
Because the goal was never to become a copy of someone else's spiritual experience.
The goal was to belong to Jesus, grow in His likeness, and serve His body through the power of the Holy Spirit.
The same Peter who once denied Jesus became a bold witness at Pentecost.
The same Paul who once persecuted the church became an apostle who taught believers to pursue love above spiritual pride.
And the same risen Christ who restored broken disciples still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
That is the Gospel.
Not a performance.
Not a competition.
Not a spiritual hierarchy.
Grace that saves.
Truth that corrects.
The Spirit who transforms.
And Jesus Christ who receives all the glory.
You were never meant to prove that you belong to Jesus by becoming someone else; you were called to follow the Savior who makes sinners new.
